sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Direct Settlement**: Revenue settlement was made directly with the **ryot** (individual cultivator), who was recognized as the proprietor of the land with rights to sell, mortgage, or lease it.
• **Absence of Intermediaries**: Unlike the Permanent Settlement, there were no **Zamindars** or revenue farmers between the state and the actual tiller of the soil.
• **Exorbitant Assessment**: Revenue demand was initially fixed very high—often **45% to 55%** of the gross produce or rental value—leaving cultivators vulnerable to severe distress.
• **Periodic Revision**: Unlike the permanent fixation in Bengal, Ryotwari rates were **subject to periodic revision** (usually every 20 to 30 years), invariably leading to hikes in revenue demands.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Madras System (Captain Alexander Read & Thomas Munro)
Implemented in major parts of Madras Presidency (1792 onwards). Focused on individual field assessment.
Survey of fields, classification of soil fertility, and fixing revenue per field payable by the occupant.
Frequent Prelims target regarding the founding architects and initial experimental districts (Baramahal).
Implemented in Bombay Presidency, Berar, and parts of Central Provinces from 1820s-1830s.
Based on survey and assessment of entire villages and holdings, using standardized soil classification.
Important for understanding the expansion of colonial control into Western India and Deccan agrarian riots.
Extended to Assam Valley in the mid-19th century due to tea plantation and wasteland expansion.
Adapted Ryotwari principles to local conditions with modified revenue rates for shifting cultivation and settled farming.
Shows spatial flexibility of the Ryotwari mechanism across diverse geographical terrains.

items.definition: The individual peasant cultivator recognized under the system as the legal owner and occupant of the land.
The registered occupant holding the patta (title deed) from the government, directly liable for revenue payment.
The rigorous process of measuring land plots, classifying soil quality, and calculating productivity to determine revenue liability.
Unlike Ryotwari (individual settlement), Mahalwari involved settlement with the village community (Mahal) as a unit through a village headman or lambardar.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Primary Regions**: Madras Presidency, Bombay Presidency, parts of Assam, and Coorg.
• **Coverage Extent**: Covered roughly **51%** of British India's territory, making it the most geographically extensive land revenue system.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Heavy cash revenue demands forced peasants into the clutches of moneylenders (Sahukars), leading to widespread rural indebtedness, land alienation, and uprisings like the **Deccan Riots of 1875**.
• **Policy Interventions**: Post-independence zamindari abolition and tenancy reforms built upon the elimination of intermediaries initiated by the historical framework, transitioning toward cooperative farming and digital land records (SVAMITVA scheme).

items.title: Mnemonic for Land Revenue Systems Coverage
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'PRIME BAZAR'
• **Decoded Meaning**: **P**ermanent = **R**engal (Bengal/Bihar), **I**ndividual/Ryotwari = **M**adras/Bombay, **E**state/Mahalwari = **N**orth-West/Punjab.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly maps each revenue system to its dominant geographical stronghold.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Ryotwari = Individual (Ryot) + Direct (No Zamindar) + Periodic Revision (Not Permanent).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that the Ryotwari system created a class of 'free peasant proprietors' who were prosperous. In reality, while individual ownership was legally recognized, crushing revenue demand and arbitrary periodic hikes drove peasants into deep debt and bondage to moneylenders, mirroring landlord exploitation.

Mains Value Addition: Quote R.C. Dutt or Dadabhai Naoroji's Drain of Wealth theory when analyzing how the rigid cash-based Ryotwari revenue demand destroyed the self-sufficient village economy and forced commercialization of agriculture.

keyTakeaways: The Ryotwari system established direct revenue settlement between the government and individual cultivators (ryots) across 51% of British India.
Pioneered by Alexander Read and Thomas Munro, it eliminated traditional intermediaries but introduced exploitative high revenue demands and periodic revisions.
Severe agrarian distress, land alienation to moneylenders, and uprisings like the Deccan Riots were direct consequences of rigid cash-based revenue extraction.
